sources.title: Human History Map: Lebanon index and border features
sources.note: Own-project factual-data exception. The imported index runs from circa 1945 to null. Six decoded polygon features cover 1945 to 2100; the historical outlines repeat in two groups and a different modern polygon begins in 2020. These shapes provide display coverage only and do not establish an independence date, exact historical frontiers, control during wars or a future endpoint.

sources.title: US Office of the Historian: Lebanon recognition and diplomatic history
sources.note: Direct US government history. The French mandate followed the First World War; the United States recognized Lebanon on 8 September 1944 and established diplomatic relations on 16 November 1944. This source addresses US recognition and relations, while a Lebanese Ministry of Finance profile supplies the separate 1943 independence and 1946 foreign-troop departure dates.

sources.title: Lebanese Ministry of Finance: Lebanon Country Profile 2014
sources.note: Direct Lebanese government country profile. Its history section dates effective political independence to 22 November 1943 and completion of foreign-troop departure to 31 December 1946. Used only for those historical milestones; its dated economic or demographic material is not reused as current evidence.

sources.title: Library of Congress: Lebanon, a country study
sources.note: Direct 1989 public-domain country study, research completed December 1987. Used only for the 1948 refugee influx, the 1958 crisis and the mounting political, social and armed tensions that led into the civil war in April 1975. Its descriptions and statistics are historical, not evidence about present-day society.

sources.title: US Office of the Historian: The Reagan Administration and Lebanon, 1981-1984
sources.note: Direct US government diplomatic history, explicitly a retired historical overview. Used for Israel's 1982 invasion, the PLO evacuation from Beirut, the entry of Israeli forces into West Beirut, the Sabra and Shatila massacre by Maronite militiamen and the multinational force. It describes US policy as well as events and is not a complete history of every civil-war faction.

sources.title: United Nations: Lebanon programme to implement the Charter of National Reconciliation
sources.note: Direct official letter from Lebanon's UN representative transmitting the Council of Ministers' 11 July 1990 implementation programme for the Taif Charter. It sought to end violence, restore constitutional authority, extend state control and require militias to hand over weapons. It records a programme and commitments, not proof that every provision was completed.

sources.title: United Nations: report of the International Independent Investigation Commission, 20 October 2005
sources.note: Direct UN commission report. Historical background states that the 1989 Taif Agreement helped end the civil war, that Syrian intelligence exercised pervasive influence and that Syrian forces withdrew in May 2005 under Security Council resolution 1559. Used narrowly for that dated transition, not as a finding about every later political relationship.

sources.title: Congressional Research Service: Lebanon, 21 April 2021
sources.note: Direct nonpartisan CRS report prepared for Congress. Its historical and political sections cover the 2005 assassination and withdrawal, the 2006 Israel-Hezbollah war, later government collapses, confessional coalitions and spillover from the Syrian conflict. Used only to characterize the unsettled 2005-2019 phase, not as a current 2026 assessment.

sources.title: World Bank: Renewed conflict derails Lebanon's fragile economic recovery, 21 August 2026
sources.note: Direct dated World Bank release for the Summer 2026 Lebanon Economic Monitor. It places the financial crisis from 2019 before a 2025 rebound and says renewed conflict from March 2026 damaged housing and infrastructure, displaced communities and interrupted recovery. The 6.4 percent contraction is a 2026 projection, not a final result.

sources.title: Presidency of the Lebanese Republic: Arabic text of the Lebanese Constitution
sources.note: Direct current Arabic constitutional text. Article 1 is marked as amended on 9 November 1943 and begins with the exact sample used in the card. Articles 10 and 11 address education and Arabic. This is a current web transcription of the amended constitution, not a facsimile of the 1943 enactment.

sources.title: Lebanese National Assembly: English text of the Lebanese Constitution
sources.note: Direct official National Assembly English constitutional text. Article 1 supplies the exact English rendering of the Arabic sample; Articles 10 and 11 cover schools and the national official language. The preamble describes a parliamentary democratic republic, and Article 24 explains equal Christian-Muslim seat allocation. Constitutional promises are legal text, not proof of equal practical access.

sources.title: UNESCO: Al-man'ouché, an emblematic culinary practice in Lebanon
sources.note: Direct UNESCO intangible-heritage listing, inscribed in 2023. Thin dough is topped with ingredients such as thyme, sumac, toasted sesame seeds, salt and olive oil; it is often served with vegetables, olives, dairy or tea. Knowledge passes in families and apprenticeships, family bakeries are common and the morning meal can bring people of different backgrounds together.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Baalbek
sources.note: Direct UNESCO World Heritage record. Describes Phoenician traditions, the Hellenistic name Heliopolis, the later Roman sanctuary, enormous monoliths and temple columns, 1984 inscription and modern Directorate General of Antiquities consolidation and restoration. Ancient construction is not credited to the modern Lebanese state; modern preservation work is.

sources.title: UNESCO: Beirut restoration and cultural recovery, 15 September 2025
sources.note: Direct dated UNESCO report. Following the 2020 port explosion and later regional hostilities, the Li Beirut response restored cultural and educational sites, supported cultural workers, trained heritage specialists, assessed damage at Tyre and Baalbek and provided storage and digitization equipment to the Directorate General of Antiquities.

sources.title: American University of Beirut Faculty of Medicine: History
sources.note: Direct institutional history. The medical school opened in 1867 and its first physicians graduated in 1871. The bacteriology department produced vaccines used by local government during the Second World War, and the medical center cared for many casualties during the Lebanese civil war. Institutional self-description is used for dated milestones, not comparative superiority claims.

sources.title: WHO Eastern Mediterranean: Lebanon and WHO launch the 2026-2029 Country Cooperation Strategy
sources.note: Direct WHO report dated 29 July 2025. The strategy was developed with Lebanon's Ministry of Public Health and prioritizes primary and hospital care, digital health, medicine management, service quality, emergency preparedness and investment in the health workforce. These are agreed priorities, not claims that all problems have been solved.

sources.title: UNESCO: Restoring Education in Beirut
sources.note: Direct UNESCO Li Beirut programme page. After the 2020 port explosions damaged schools, vocational centres and universities, UNESCO and partners completed rehabilitation of 280 educational institutions within 18 months; direct work included 95 schools, 20 vocational institutions, 30 university buildings and eleven school libraries. Figures describe this programme, not every damaged building.

sources.title: UNICEF Lebanon: Lebanon's schools caught in the crossfire, September 2026
sources.note: Direct UNICEF and Ministry of Education evidence published September 2026. A survey assessed 1,089 educational facilities after hostilities beginning 2 March 2026 and recorded 436 damaged and 37 destroyed. Response options included in-person, distance and blended learning plus psychosocial and inclusion support. This is a dated wartime assessment.

sources.title: UNICEF Lebanon: Beirut Explosion response
sources.note: Direct UNICEF programme record after the August 2020 port explosions. More than 1,900 young people joined community response, including trained vocational students; work included debris removal, minor repairs, meals and masks. UNICEF and partners also supported child protection, schools, health facilities, water connections and sanitation. Numbers are programme outputs, not the entire city response.

sources.title: UNICEF Lebanon: Water, Sanitation and Hygiene Programme
sources.note: Direct current programme page. It describes unreliable pumping and treatment since the 2019 economic crisis, dependence on private water trucks, poorly functioning wastewater plants and 2024 conflict pressure. Dated results include toilets and showers in shelters, more than 500 water-system repairs in 2024 and support to rehabilitate 16 wastewater facilities by 2025.

sources.title: UNICEF Lebanon: Emergency response in Lebanon
sources.note: Direct UNICEF response page for the 2024 displacement emergency. It records sanitation and hygiene improvements at 187 displacement sites through 713 showers and 413 toilets. This is a specific humanitarian intervention, not a national household-toilet count or a claim that temporary facilities solved the wider water crisis.

proposedOverrides.name: Lebanon
proposedOverrides.summary: Lebanon: an independent parliamentary republic shaped by civil war, reconstruction and new crises, with archaeology, family bakeries, Arabic writing, medical education, classrooms and sanitation in daily life.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: One coherent modern-state card across the indexed lebanon record. Independence in 1943, US recognition in 1944, the atlas's circa-1945 opening and French troop withdrawal in 1946 are explicitly distinguished. Ancient Phoenician, Hellenistic and Roman societies are context for heritage only, not merged into the republic.
batchIdentityNotes.geometry: Six polygon features decoded. The 1945-1960 and 1960-1994 features share bbox [34.97254972549726,32.907358927702205,36.502565025650256,34.5320752404443] and repeat the same historical outline. The 1994-2000, 2000-2010 and 2010-2020 features share the near-identical bbox [34.97254972549726,32.90633861825308,36.502565025650256,34.53184310055237]. A simpler replacement polygon covers 2020-2100 with bbox [35.126,33.089,36.612,34.645]. Imported coordinates remain unchanged; none is used to infer wartime control or a future border.
batchIdentityNotes.chronology: Mandate ended in 1943, US recognition followed in 1944 and French forces withdrew in 1946. Interpretive phases then mark the 1958 crisis, 1975-1990 civil war, Taif implementation, Syrian withdrawal in 2005, financial crisis from 2019, 2020 port explosions and dated 2026 conflict evidence. Phase boundaries are historical reading aids, not alternate geometry claims.
batchIdentityNotes.writing: Exact nine-word Arabic opening of Constitution Article 1 paired with the official Constitutional Council English rendering. The card identifies right-to-left direction and Article 11 language status. It is a current typed constitutional witness to a provision amended in 1943, not an original manuscript or ancient inscription.
batchIdentityNotes.sourceBoundaries: Historical Library of Congress and Office of the Historian sources are confined to past events. World Bank, UNICEF and WHO claims carry publication or assessment dates. Baalbek's ancient construction is not credited to the modern state; conservation is. School, volunteer and sanitation figures are bounded to named programmes and emergencies rather than generalized nationally.
